drills.q: Explain BPE end to end: how is the vocabulary built, and how is a new word encoded?
drills.a: Start with a base alphabet (bytes/chars); repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent symbol pair into a new symbol, recording the rule in order, until vocab hits target size. To encode new text, replay the learned merges in training order against the new text's base-symbol sequence until none apply -- no frequency counting at encode time.

drills.q: Why is byte-level BPE the standard for production LLM tokenizers rather than character-level?
drills.a: Base alphabet is the 256 byte values -- every Unicode character in any script decomposes to 1-4 UTF-8 bytes, so any input is representable with no <UNK> fallback. Character-level BPE must cover 140,000+ Unicode code points and rare characters may never earn merges.

drills.q: What's actually different between BPE, WordPiece, and SentencePiece?
drills.a: BPE merges the most frequent adjacent pair; WordPiece merges by max corpus likelihood under a unigram LM (small practical difference). SentencePiece isn't a competing algorithm -- it's a library implementing BPE or Unigram over the raw byte/Unicode stream, treating whitespace as an ordinary symbol, which is why it's the multilingual default.

drills.q: Why do tokens not correspond to words, and what determines whether a word is one token or several?
drills.a: A token is whatever chunk accumulated enough BPE merges during training -- purely frequency-driven, no linguistic notion of 'word'. Common words in the dominant training language merge fully into one token; rare words or words in underrepresented languages fragment into multiple subword tokens.

drills.q: A user reports identical requests in English and Hindi are priced very differently. Diagnose it.
drills.a: Likely tokenizer fragmentation: if the tokenizer's training corpus was English-dominated, Hindi words never earned full BPE merges and decompose into many more subword/byte tokens for the same content, inflating token-based cost. Confirm by measuring tokens-per-sentence for matched content in both languages against the exact tokenizer in use.

drills.q: What happens when a tokenizer encounters a completely novel string or random bytes -- does it ever fail?
drills.a: Never fails outright with byte-level BPE: the string decomposes to its base byte sequence and learned merges apply wherever they match; unmatched bytes remain individual byte-tokens. No <UNK> fallback needed since the byte alphabet is complete by construction -- but novel text uses more tokens per character, the same mechanism behind the multilingual cost problem.

drills.q: Explain why vocabulary size is a real tradeoff, not 'bigger is strictly better'.
drills.a: Larger vocab reduces tokens-per-word (cheaper inference, more effective context) but the embedding table and output projection scale with vocab_size * d_model, directly growing parameter count and per-step softmax compute. GPT-2's 50k vs GPT-4o's ~200k (o200k_base) trades shorter sequences against real parameter/compute cost.

drills.q: How do special tokens like <eos>/<bos>/chat-template markers interact with BPE merging, and what breaks if templating gets whitespace wrong?
drills.a: Special tokens are matched as literal atomic strings before BPE merging runs and never fragment. But tokens adjacent to them can tokenize differently depending on surrounding whitespace (since leading space is often part of the following word's leading symbol in byte-level BPE), producing a token sequence the model never saw in training -- looks like a model regression but is a templating bug.

drills.q: Fine-tuning a base model on a new low-resource language or heavily code-mixed domain gives poor results despite plenty of data. What tokenizer-level cause would you check first?
drills.a: Check tokens-per-sentence for the new domain against the base tokenizer -- heavy fragmentation means the model spends context budget reconstructing fragmented subwords instead of modeling the domain, which more fine-tuning data alone can't fix. Requires vocabulary extension (add tokens, resize embeddings, continue pretraining) or a domain-adapted tokenizer.

drills.q: Design a tokenizer strategy for a product shipping across 22 locales with a strict per-request cost/latency SLA.
drills.a: Measure actual tokens-per-equivalent-sentence for each locale against the exact tokenizer in use, rather than assuming a uniform ratio. Set per-locale cost/context-length budgets from that measured data. If certain locales are severely underserved, factor tokenizer/vocab balance into model/vendor selection -- this can't be patched at the serving layer once a model is chosen.
